SwimHR: Wearable-Free Heart Rate Monitoring for Swimmers via Water-Mediated ECG Sensing

the first wearable-free HR monitoring system that captures electrocardiogram (ECG) signals transmitted through pool water without any on-body device
Jiting Liu1  ·  Yue Gong1  ·  Zeyu Luo1  ·  Billy Chun Lung So2  ·  Qijia Shao1
1 The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology2 The Hong Kong Polytechnic University

What it is

The paper's story: where it is used, its core idea and the real system demo.
Real-world use

Heart rate of a swimmer, read through the pool water

Imagine the idea beyond the pool, where the Sensing World places it; the paper itself tested two public pools.

Park and lake · Lake · Sensing World ›
Motivation

Heart-rate wearables are problematic underwater

  1. 1ECG chest straps must be worn tightly, which is often uncomfortable and distracting
  2. 2photoplethysmography (PPG) sensors suffer severe accuracy degradation due to swimming-induced motion artifacts
  3. 3current wearables mostly expose HR only after the session
what each wearable reads

It shows What each earlier way reads in the water: a chest strap's clean ECG, then a forearm PPG sensor's rate lagging the truth in butterfly.

How to read it The solid line is what the wearable gives and the dashed line the true heart rate, so where they part the wearable is wrong.

State of the art

ECG through water had been shown only in confined settings

  1. 1Prior studies have shown that ECG can propagate through water, but only in very confined settings
  2. 2with stationary users and electrodes placed close to the body
  3. 3These feasibility demonstrations do not address the conditions that matter in real swimming

It shows Before SwimHR, the heart was read through water in confined settings such as bathtubs, from still people with electrodes close by.

How to read it Right is a longer way from the body to the electrodes; up is from a still bather to a swimmer in a lane.

Background

Four terms used throughout

ECG and R-peak01

the R-peak in the QRS complex is widely used for heart-rate (HR) estimation

Water-mediated ECG02

When the body is immersed in water, the cardiac electrical field can propagate into the surrounding conductive medium

Cardiac dipole03

We then model the heart as a dipole with a positive and a negative pole

Bias (DRL) electrode04

ECG front-ends typically rely on a third bias (driven-right-leg) electrode in skin contact

one heartbeat in the ECG

It shows One heartbeat as an ECG draws it: the small P wave, the sharp QRS spike with its R-peak, then the T wave.

How to read it Time runs left to right; the gap between two R-peaks (RR) gives the heart rate: 60 divided by RR in seconds.

Core idea

Electrodes along the lane read the heart through the water

  1. 1use pool water itself as the sensing medium for ECG
  2. 2electrodes closer to the swimmer experience a higher electric potential than those farther away
  3. 3allowing ECG sensing through the spatial potential gradient along the swimming lane
the potential along the rope

It shows The heart's potential at each of the 25 electrodes, highest under the swimmer, and the difference one pair 3 m apart reads.

How to read it Bars: the potential at each electrode as the swimmer passes; the line below: the pair's difference over time, the ECG.

Core idea · what to observe

The heartbeat moves from channel to channel with the swimmer

the ECG signal strength shifts across sensing channels

ECG signals are typically observable in three adjacent channels at a time

  1. The swimmer passes over the rope's electrodes
  2. Near channels show the beat; far ones stay flat
  3. The strongest channels travel along with the swimmer
  4. Your turn Drag the swimmer along the lane
Swimmer's place –

the 13 channels

It shows Each row is one channel's ECG over the last 4 s; only the channels near the swimmer show clear beats.

How to read it C1 at the top to C13 at the bottom, in lane order; the three lit rows are the strongest; flat rows are too far away.

ECG per channel

It shows The ECG's size on each channel: a bump that moves along the lane with the swimmer.

How to read it One bar per channel, C1 to C13, μV peak to peak; lit: the adjacent three of largest sum, so one may sit below a grey bar.

Challenge 1 · weak signal

A pool weakens the heart's signal far more than a bathtub

pool-scale water-mediated ECG is extremely weak and strongly environment-dependent

In a bathtub with the same subject and 0.5 m electrode spacing, the amplitude reaches 688.1 μV but drops to 98.3 μV in the pool

  1. New: a bathtub, its two electrodes 0.5 m apart
  2. In the tub, the ECG is large and clear
  3. The same pair in a pool: about seven times smaller
  4. Farther electrodes: weaker still
Measured now –
ECG (μV) against spacing

It shows The ECG falls as the electrodes move away from the body; at 0.5 m the pool gives 98.3 μV, seven times less than a bathtub.

How to read it x: electrode spacing, m; y: ECG peak to peak, μV; line: the dipole model fitted to Fig. 3(b); dots and ring: the paper's pool values.

the ECG received

It shows Beats of the same heart in a bathtub and in a pool, on one scale: the pool's beats are about 7 times smaller.

How to read it μV over the last 4 s; tall beats: the bathtub, 688.1 μV; small beats between them: the pool, 98.3 μV; bright: the setting now.

Solution 1 · transmission model

A dipole model of ECG transmission in pool water

ECG transmission in pool water can be modeled as a quasi-static conduction process

  1. New: the heart as two poles of current
  2. An electrode's voltage falls with distance to each pole
  3. The fitted model runs through the measured points
  4. A bigger pool and a grounded ladder cut the ECG more
  5. Your turn Change each factor
Model now –
Paper, Fig. 3(b) –
ECG, μV, and paper points

It shows At one conductivity, 0.045 S/m, the fitted dipole model runs through the paper's points: the ECG falls as the electrodes move away.

How to read it x: the geometric term from each electrode's distance to the poles, 1/m; y: ECG, μV; dots: the paper's; line and ring: the model now.

ECG, μV, by pool size

It shows A bigger pool and a grounded ladder each cut the ECG; higher conductivity, the σ slider, is the paper's third factor.

How to read it x: the simulated pool's side, m; y: ECG, μV; dots: the paper's simulation; line: the model; dashed: with the ladder; upright line: now.

Challenge 2 · full-lane coverage

One electrode pair covers only a few metres of the lane

monitoring a swimmer during laps requires full-lane coverage

standard ECG front-ends typically rely on a third bias (driven-right-leg) electrode in skin contact to stabilize the input common-mode voltage and prevent ADC saturation

  1. New: one pair of electrodes at mid-lane
  2. The beat shows only while the swimmer is near it
  3. With no electrode on the body, the common mode drifts
  4. Past the converter's limit the channel saturates
Lane covered –
Common mode –
one pair, μV

It shows One pair hears the swimmer only over a few metres of the 25 m lane; elsewhere its ECG is under the floor.

How to read it x: swimmer's place, m; y: the pair's ECG, μV; dots: the run, red at 0 when saturated; dashed: 1 μV floor; shaded: heard.

common mode, V

It shows With no bias electrode the inputs float, so the common mode drifts past the chip's limits and the channel saturates.

How to read it y: the common-mode voltage, V, over the last 20 s, the supplies at its ends; dashed lines: the ADS1299's limits; red: past them.

Solution 2 · lane-scale hardware

Same-side rope electrodes and a bias-electrode-free circuit

These resistors provide a weak bias path that stabilizes the input common-mode voltage without requiring direct body-electrode contact.

  1. New: 25 electrodes on one rope, 1 m apart
  2. Pairs 3 m apart make 13 channels
  3. Some channel always hears the swimmer
  4. New: 10 MΩ resistors hold the common mode
  5. Your turn Each part off and on
Lane covered –
Common mode –
25 electrodes, 13 pairs

It shows Fig. 4's layout: 25 electrodes 1 m apart, paired 3 m apart in four groups plus E22–E25, make 13 channels.

How to read it E1 to E25 along the rope; each arc a channel, as Fig. 4; bold: the channels chosen now; triangle: the swimmer.

best channel, μV

It shows With 13 channels some channel carries the beat wherever the swimmer is, so the whole lane is covered.

How to read it x: the swimmer's place along the lane, m; y: the best channel's ECG, μV; dots: the run; dashed: the 1 μV floor; shaded: heard.

common mode, V

It shows The 10 MΩ bias path holds the common mode inside the chip's limits, so the channel does not saturate.

How to read it y: the common-mode voltage, V, over the last 20 s, the supplies at its ends; dashed lines: the ADS1299's limits; red: past them.

Challenge 3 · swimming artifacts

Each stroke disturbs the signal in its own way

Different strokes and intensities induce qualitatively different artifact patterns, which can obscure QRS complexes and cause false peaks or missed beats

these artifacts vary across strokes, making fixed-threshold peak detection unreliable

  1. New: butterfly, the hardest stroke
  2. A fixed threshold takes artifacts for beats
  3. It also misses beats the artifacts hide
  4. So the heart rate jumps off the truth
True HR –
Fixed-threshold HR –
Error now –
butterfly, the hardest stroke: the chosen channel

It shows In butterfly, motion artifacts are as tall as beats, so a fixed threshold misses beats and takes artifacts for beats.

How to read it The chosen channel's last 4 s, μV; triangles: beats found; crosses: false beats; rings: beats missed.

butterfly: HR (bpm) against truth

It shows The fixed-threshold heart rate strays from the true one, often by several bpm.

How to read it bpm over the last 30 s; solid: the true HR (shaped as Fig. 9); dashed: the fixed-threshold estimate.

Solution 3 · spatial–temporal extraction

Spatial–temporal heart-rate extraction

The improvement is most pronounced for butterfly, where MAE decreases from 2.46 ± 2.47 bpm to 1.56 ± 1.25 bpm

  1. Stage 1: three adjacent channels chosen
  2. Stage 2: the U-Net marks R-peaks (Fig. 5)
  3. Stage 3: odd peaks and jumps filtered out
  4. Butterfly still errs most: reduced, not removed
  5. Your turn Each stage off and on; a stroke

Ablation study

Question What does each part of SwimHR add to the heart rate?Every try is the same butterfly swim, the paper's hardest stroke. The paper tests NeuroKit2 in place of the U-Net in every stroke (Table 2), and filtering off on breaststroke (§5.3); switching off channel selection, polarity or the bias path is this model's own test.

You change
SwimHR's parts, one off at a time

Why it matters Each part answers a problem: a floating input, a moving swimmer, a beat flipped at each turn, weak beats, stray peaks.The error is how far SwimHR's heart rate is from the chest strap's, on average, as the paper measures it. Both runs swim the same laps.

  1. 1Your turn PressOff, SwimHR reads three fixed channels in the middle of the lane, C6 to C8. The swimmer leaves them for most of each lap.
  2. 2Your turn PressNeuroKit2 is the paper's baseline; here a fixed-threshold peak finder stands in for it. The U-Net is not run: true beats count as found, a few missed and a few false, at the paper's breaststroke rate, more in butterfly (assumed).
  3. 3Your turn PressWithout stage 3, one false or missed peak changes the last three RR intervals, and the heart rate jumps.
  4. 4Your turn PressThe 10 MΩ resistors hold the inputs' common mode. Without them it drifts until the ADC saturates, after about 7 s (the drift is assumed).

What you saw Error: the mean gap to the strap's heart rate over the last 30 s, each try on the same laps. The artifacts' sizes are assumed; the paper's butterfly MAE is 1.56 bpm with the U-Net and 2.46 bpm with NeuroKit2 (Table 2).ECG signals are typically observable in three adjacent channels at a time, while signals in distant channels are too weak to detect the U-Net provides more accurate R-peak detection than the conventional baseline, while temporal consistency filtering further reduces residual detection errors the temporal filtering reduces false detections and prevents error propagation during brief signal loss These resistors provide a weak bias path that stabilizes the input common-mode voltage without requiring direct body-electrode contact the U-Net yields lower mean MAE in every category and lower variability in most cases

Question How does SwimHR compare with what swimmers wear today?SwimHR here is our simulation. The chest strap is our dipole model read at the skin. The three PPG wearables are the paper's own measured errors (Fig. 8).

What you saw The PPG errors are the paper's means over its swims, not our simulation. The chest strap is the paper's ground truth: its error is zero by definition, but it is worn tight (§1).commonly used PPG-based wearables exhibit substantially higher errors and larger performance variability, with further degradation during high-motion strokes such as butterfly the temple-mounted PPG sensor shows an MAE of 8.9 bpm for amateur breaststroke but improves to 2.7 bpm for professional swimmers The Polar Verity Sense provides denser HR estimates but remains sensitive to motion artifacts and sensor placement variability. unlike the evaluated wearables, including the ground-truth ECG chest band, which store data locally and provide HR only after the swimming session, SwimHR places its acquisition and wireless communication units on the pool deck

Go Beyond the Paper · 1 of 3

Generalization study

Question How far from the rope does SwimHR still read the heart?The paper's swimmers stayed within ±1.25 m of the rope, with the electrodes 1 m down. Here the swimmer goes up to 4 m across, the electrodes down to 3 m.

You change
the swimmer's distance, the electrodes' depth, the heart rate, a second swimmer

Why it matters The paper's swimmers stayed within 1.25 m of the rope, so no test says how far the beat still reaches a channel.Algorithm 1 keeps a peak only when it is over 1 μV and 6 dB above its sides. Past that, the channels carry noise alone.

  1. 1Your turn PressAt 2.5 m the swimmer is in the next lane, twice as far across as the paper's swimmers went.
  2. 2Your turn PressA competition pool is deeper than the paper's 1.6 m. With the rope held lower, its electrodes sit farther from the heart; the paper leaves the mounts there to future work.
  3. 3Your turn PressAlgorithm 1 accepts a heart rate only between 60 and 200 bpm, so it refuses one past that.
  4. 4Your turn Switch onA second swimmer swims beside the first, its heart at 118 bpm (assumed). Fig. 12 shows two still swimmers' beats on one channel.

What you saw Lane covered: the share of the 25 m where some channel's beat passes Algorithm 1's two floors, 1 μV and 6 dB. Past the paper's 1.25 m, every number here is the model's.the target swimmer remained within ±1.25 m of the sensing electrodes the target swimmer remained within ±1.25 m of the sensing electrodes We evaluate SwimHR only in pools up to 1.6 m deep, using a research prototype that holds the electrodes 1 m below the water surface The signal captured by the lane-rope channel shows a mixture of ECG waveforms from both swimmers

lane covered, %, or the mixed channel

It shows How much of the lane a channel hears the heart in as the swimmer moves away; with two swimmers, both hearts on one channel.

HR against truth

It shows SwimHR's heart rate beside the true one: far away, too fast, or with two hearts, it strays or stops.

Go Beyond the Paper · 2 of 3

Physical conditions

Question Which pool conditions change SwimHR's heart rate, and which do not?Each control is one thing a pool or the board can differ in. The swimmer swims breaststroke laps 0.5 m from the rope.

You change
the water, the pool's size and steel, the mains, the sampling rate

Why it matters Pools differ in water, size and steel; the water, the size and a ladder change how much signal reaches the rope.The paper simulated pools 0.5 to 9 m a side, then a 5 m pool for the water and the steel (App. A). Rebar changed the signal very little. In its two real pools, three swimmers' mean error was 1.02 and 0.68 bpm (Table 3).

  1. 1Your turn PressConductivity σ says how well the water carries current. In the paper's Eq. 4, the ECG is the heart's current over 4πσ times a distance term, so more σ means a weaker ECG.
  2. 2Your turn PressThe paper's simulation shrinks the pool round the same body. In a small pool the current has less water to spread through, so more reaches the electrodes.
  3. 3Your turn Switch onThree steel steps at 0 V in the pool's corner, as in Fig. 14(b). They drain current that would reach the electrodes.
  4. 4Your turn Raise the mains to 20 μV.Mains: the 50 Hz hum of the building's power, the same at every electrode. The paper does not measure it. The 10–30 Hz band-pass keeps almost none of 50 Hz.
More controls
Sampling rate
Strongest channel, lap peak –
HR error, last 20 s –
Mains in a channel, raw –
R-peak timing error –

What you saw The pool's size, the ladder and the rebar act as factors read off the paper's simulation, not a field solved here. The mains level and the 250 Hz rate go past the paper (assumed).Higher water conductivity further attenuates the signal, as σ appears in the denominator of Equation 4 these results indicate that SwimHR maintains reliable HR estimation across swimming pool environments the attenuation rate plateaus once dimensions exceed 3 m × 3 m pool ladders significantly decrease V pp to 66 μV, reducing signal strength to 38% of the original value The reinforcing bars reduce V pp from 176 μV to 172 μV, causing negligible signal attenuation

Optimal array setup design

Question Where should the rope electrodes go, and how far apart should a pair be?Each channel reads the difference between two electrodes on the rope. A swimmer far from every channel gives no heart rate.

Fixed
the water and the stroke
You change
the electrodes and the pair separation
You watch
the lane covered and the weakest signal
  1. 1Your turn Drag an electrode along the rope.Drag one off the lane to take it away.
  2. 2Your turn Move the pair separation away from 3 m.
  3. 3Your turn Take electrodes away with their slider.
  4. 4Your turn Press25 electrodes 1 m apart from 0.5 m, in four groups, each pairing three electrodes with the ones 3 m on, and E22 with E25, so 13 channels (Fig. 4).
More controls
Lane covered paper full lane–
Weakest signal along the lane –
Channels paper 13–
HR error, last 30 s –

What you saw A wider pair gives a larger signal, but the motion noise at its two electrodes is less alike, so less of it cancels. The chain sets that noise so a 3 m pair is best (assumed).Our measurements show that a 3 m separation provides the best trade-off between signal strength and motion robustness

the lane from above, m · colour: the best channel's signal

It shows How strong the best channel's signal is with the swimmer's heart at each place in the lane: a red band is a gap in coverage.

How to read it The lane from above in metres: rings are electrodes on the rope, arcs join each channel's pair, and gold means a strong signal.
